title: Four ways to notice a visible detail
description: Private source-review example: compare or eye-trace visible edges and surface patterns from one safe seated or standing spot. Not an approved public family/teacher pack or a field-tested result.

author.name: Pocket Field Trip project author (confirmation pending)

cards.title: Find two kinds of edge
cards.subtitle: Where one thing becomes another.
cards.meaning: Observe the edges and boundaries between ordinary outdoor surfaces from a safe stationary place. Compare a straight border with an uneven border using your eyes. A five minute visual creative contrast, without touching or approaching water.
steps: Settle in a safe spot, seated or standing, away from traffic and water’s edge. Use only what is already in view. If nothing suitable is visible, stop and choose another note; do not move closer.
Choose two visible edges where one surface meets another. Compare their shapes: which is straighter, and which has more surprises?
Look once more without moving closer. Keep one contrast in mind, or bring it back as a sentence. Leave the scene untouched.
cards.prompt: Which edge was more orderly, and which surprised you?
cards.takeaway: Bring back a sentence about where things meet.
cards.rationale: Two visible boundaries give a concrete shape comparison. A contrast sentence records the difference; the same stationary safety rule applies in every setting.

cards.title: Follow an edge with your eyes
cards.subtitle: A small journey while staying still.
cards.meaning: Follow a visible edge or boundary with your eyes from a safe stationary outdoor spot. Trace how a line bends, breaks or changes without touching objects or moving toward it. A five minute drawing-inspired observation of ordinary shapes.
steps: Settle in a safe spot, seated or standing, away from traffic and water’s edge. Use only what is already in view. If nothing suitable is visible, stop and choose another note; do not move closer.
Choose one visible edge. Follow it with your eyes. Notice one bend, break or change in direction.
Imagine that change as a tiny drawn mark. Keep it in mind, or describe it in a sentence later. Leave the scene untouched.
cards.prompt: What shape would capture the edge you followed?
cards.takeaway: Bring back the shape of a line you had overlooked.
cards.rationale: A single visible boundary supports eye-only tracing. An imagined mark records its bend; this is an alternative in the same boundaries family, not a fresh family.

cards.title: Compare two surfaces
cards.subtitle: A touch-free texture study.
cards.meaning: Notice textures without walking or touching anything. Compare two outdoor surfaces visible from one safe spot, such as paving, a wall or a railing. Study rough and smooth patterns with your eyes. Five minute creative observation without needing plants.
steps: Settle in a safe spot, seated or standing, away from traffic and water’s edge. Use only what is already in view. If nothing suitable is visible, stop and choose another note; do not move closer.
Choose two surfaces already in view. Compare rough and smooth patterns using only the details you can make out.
Choose two describing words, one for each surface. Keep them in mind, or write them later. Leave both untouched.
cards.prompt: What two words describe the surfaces you compared?
cards.takeaway: Bring back a pair of words for an ordinary place.
cards.rationale: Two already-visible surfaces support visual comparison without touching. A pair of words gives each surface a trace; plants and direct light are not prerequisites.

cards.title: Follow a surface pattern
cards.subtitle: One small line in an ordinary surface.
cards.meaning: Follow a visible line in an outdoor surface pattern with your eyes from a safe seated or standing spot. Notice a bend or break in paving, a wall or a railing without touching, walking closer or needing plants. Imagine one tiny mark for a five minute visual texture observation.
steps: Settle in a safe spot, seated or standing, away from traffic and water’s edge. Use only what is already in view. If nothing suitable is visible, stop and choose another note; do not move closer.
Choose one line in a visible surface pattern. Follow it with your eyes. Notice one bend, break or change in direction.
Imagine that change as a tiny drawn mark. Keep it in mind, or describe it in a sentence later. Leave the scene untouched.
cards.prompt: What bend or break did you notice in the surface pattern?
cards.takeaway: Bring back the shape of a line you had overlooked.
cards.rationale: A line already visible in a surface pattern makes eye-only tracing concrete. It reuses the shape trace and remains in the surface-pair family, so it cannot bypass recent or set-aside surface feedback.
